articles.title: Three checks to run yourself before accepting a CRM integration
articles.excerpt: "Integration complete" is the most expensive sentence in a form-to-CRM project, because no test is attached to it. Two failures cause most of the damage after handover: Duplicates — the same lead is w…
articles.body: "Integration complete" is the most expensive sentence in a form-to-CRM project, because no test is attached to it. Two failures cause most of the damage after handover: Duplicates — the same lead is written twice (double submit, retry, or a webhook delivered twice). Silent loss — the CRM returns 5xx for a few seconds and the lead disappears while the visitor sees an error page. Both pass every live demo, because a demo submits once and the CRM is healthy. So before accepting, run three scenarios in a test environment and record four columns: input, expected, actual, verdict. I ran this against a mock CRM with synthetic data ( OBS-001 , OBS-002 ) on 2026-11-21; every number below came from that run log.

articles.title: A 5-Step Preflight for Desktop Automation Before Real Data
articles.excerpt: Desktop automation often fails at the boundaries: the app opens slowly, a dialog appears, a row is malformed, or a previous run stopped after saving only part of the work. A safe first run makes those…
articles.body: Desktop automation often fails at the boundaries: the app opens slowly, a dialog appears, a row is malformed, or a previous run stopped after saving only part of the work. A safe first run makes those conditions visible before the workflow touches production data. Here is a practical preflight you can use with a macro, an RPA tool, or a visual workflow builder. 1. Write the success condition Describe the input, the expected destination state, and a clear stop condition. “Fill in the form” is too vague. “Create one record with these three fields, then confirm the record appears in the results list” is checkable. 2. Build a small test fixture Use a copy or synthetic data. Include one valid case, one missing value, and one duplicate. Keep the first run small enough to inspect by hand.

articles.body: Originally published on OKAIHub . A solo founder either obsesses over metrics daily, which is demoralising because nothing moves that fast, or avoids them entirely, which means decisions get made on feeling. A weekly review is the middle path: frequent enough to catch problems, infrequent enough that the numbers have had time to mean something. This is a thirty-minute format that produces one decision, not a dashboard you glance at and forget. Why weekly and not daily Daily numbers are noise. A single day's traffic or signups varies for reasons that have nothing to do with what you did. Reading them daily produces emotional decisions. Weekly shows a trend.

articles.body: AI agents ask for passwords. I made sure they never see them How to give an AI agent access to secrets without leaking them. Based on a real product: TenVault 1.0 / AgentVault (Windows, Rust + Tauri). The problem that arrived quietly A year ago an "AI agent" was a toy: it wrote code and sometimes hallucinated. Today agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code extensions, custom bots) work on real projects — which means they need keys and passwords : OpenAI, Stripe, databases, staging environments. The usual workarounds are bad: .env in the project. The agent reads it. Best case it does not decide to "improve" the config or paste it into a 100k-token context. Copy the key into a prompt. It lands in logs, chat history and the provider's cache. Game over. A cloud secrets manager.

articles.body: "You have 2 free articles left this month." Metered paywalls are common on news sites, newsletters, course platforms, and documentation portals. Many of them do the counting in the browser: a cookie or localStorage entry holds the number of articles read, and a script decides whether to show the overlay. That design is popular because it is cheap and works with aggressive CDN caching. It also means the reader controls the counter, and often the full article is already in the HTML under the overlay. articles.title: Parallelization Workflow with Spring AI: Fan-Out LLM Calls in Java
articles.excerpt: When people first start building with LLMs in Java, the usual shape of the code is simple: build a prompt, call the model, read the answer. That works well for a single question. It starts to hurt whe…
articles.body: When people first start building with LLMs in Java, the usual shape of the code is simple: build a prompt, call the model, read the answer. That works well for a single question. It starts to hurt when you need to ask the same model the same kind of question a hundred times, or when one request is really five smaller questions that happen to be asked together. Each call waits for the network, the model generates tokens at its own pace, and your thread sits idle for most of that time. Anthropic's article "Building Effective Agents" describes a set of workflow patterns for composing LLM calls. One of them is the Parallelization Workflow : instead of running model calls one after another, you run them at the same time and then combine the results.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of lightwhile observing Jupiter and its moon volcanic moon Io. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

articles.body: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .

articles.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo probe arrives in orbit around Mercury today
articles.excerpt: The BepiColombo spacecraft will finally arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.
articles.body: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

articles.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.
articles.body: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on Nov. 20, 2026.
